title: Foundations: Starlight Tales - The Complete Guide
summary: What Starlight Tales books are, where the genre came from, and how to read them.
body:
Starlight Tales: Children's literature is where the great fantasies live: Wonderland, Oz, Neverland, Pooh Corner. The best children's books are written with full artistry and no condescension.

History: Alice (1865) proved children's books could be literature. The Edwardian golden age - Barrie, Grahame, Milne, Potter - built the canon; the form has never looked back.

HOW TO READ THIS SHELF: start with the landmark titles below — each record carries the complete plot, themes, a quoted passage, and craft notes. Read foundations first, then follow the ladder: compounded titles deepen the form, advanced titles challenge it.

# Starlight Tales foundations: reading-plan calculator
def reading_plan(total_pages, pages_per_day, days_per_week=7):
    days = total_pages / pages_per_day
    weeks = days / days_per_week
    return days, weeks

def session_words(words_per_minute=250, minutes=30):
    return words_per_minute * minutes

for pages in [200, 300, 400]:
    d, w = reading_plan(pages, 30)
    print(f'{pages} pages at 30/day: {d:.0f} days (~{w:.1f} weeks)')
print('30-min session at 250 wpm:', session_words(), 'words')
program.note: Estimates reading schedules from page counts and pace.

title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for Alice's Adventures in Wonderland by Lewis Carroll (1865): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Alice's Adventures in Wonderland by Lewis Carroll (1865). Shelf fit: The dream book.

COMPLETE PLOT: Alice follows the White Rabbit into a world of mad tea parties and mock-turtle soup, growing and shrinking through logic turned upside down - then wakes on the riverbank.

THEMES: Logic, language, and growing up.

FROM THE TEXT: "Curiouser and curiouser!"

CRAFT NOTE: Carroll's rule: the dream must have rules, or it's just noise.

body:
Winnie-the-Pooh by A. A. Milne (1926). Shelf fit: The Bear of Very Little Brain.

COMPLETE PLOT: Pooh, Piglet, Eeyore, and Christopher Robin have gentle adventures in the Hundred Acre Wood - hunts for heffalumps, Eeyore's birthdays, Pooh's poems. Public domain in the US since 2022.

THEMES: Friendship and the wisdom of simplicity.

FROM THE TEXT: "A bear, however hard he tries, grows tubby without exercise."

CRAFT NOTE: Milne's tone: the narrator loves his characters exactly as they are.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARLIGHT TALES SHELF: The Bear of Very Little Brain. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

Peter Pan by J. M. Barrie (1911). Shelf fit: Neverland.

COMPLETE PLOT: Peter lures Wendy, John, and Michael to Neverland - pirates, mermaids, lost boys, Hook. Wendy mothers them; Peter forgets, because forgetting is his gift.

FROM THE TEXT: "All children, except one, grow up."

CRAFT NOTE: Barrie's Neverland: childhood as a country with geography.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARLIGHT TALES SHELF: Neverland. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

summary: Full record for The Tale of Peter Rabbit by Beatrix Potter (1902): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Tale of Peter Rabbit by Beatrix Potter (1902). Shelf fit: The naughty rabbit.

COMPLETE PLOT: Peter disobeys his mother, squeezes under the McGregors' gate, gorges on lettuces, and barely escapes - to chamomile tea and bed. Potter's precise natural history inside mischief.

THEMES: Disobedience and consequence, gently.

FROM THE TEXT: "Now run along, and don't get into mischief."

CRAFT NOTE: Potter's science: every rabbit, mouse, and hedgehog is accurately observed.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARLIGHT TALES SHELF: The naughty rabbit. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

Five Children and It by E. Nesbit (1902). Shelf fit: Wishes with consequences.

COMPLETE PLOT: Five siblings find a grumpy sand-fairy granting one wish a day till sunset. Wishes for beauty, wealth, and flight all backfire instructively.

THEMES: Wishes have consequences; real children in magic.

FROM THE TEXT: "Nesbit's children: quarrelsome, real, and utterly believable."

CRAFT NOTE: Nesbit's innovation: real children inside the fantasy.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARLIGHT TALES SHELF: Wishes with consequences. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

The Secret Garden by Frances Hodgson Burnett (1911). Shelf fit: The garden that heals.

CRAFT NOTE: Burnett's garden: the setting as the second protagonist.

The Velveteen Rabbit by Margery Williams (1922). Shelf fit: Becoming real.

COMPLETE PLOT: A shabby toy rabbit learns that becoming Real happens when a child loves you - and is made real by magic at the end.

FROM THE TEXT: "Real isn't how you are made. It's a thing that happens to you."

CRAFT NOTE: Williams's gentleness: the quietest fantasy, the deepest theme.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE STARLIGHT TALES SHELF: Becoming real. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
